### On Paying Attention

One afternoon last autumn, I was waiting at a bus stop in a city I had recently moved to. There was a maple tree nearby, its leaves a complicated shade of amber and rust. I had no phone to fill the minutes, so I looked. Then I did what felt strange: I kept looking. For perhaps seven minutes I watched the wind work through the leaves, saw some spin slowly downward, others drop like stones, and noticed how fallen leaves rearranged themselves on the sidewalk in small eddies. A woman passed with a stroller; a leaf landed on her baby’s blanket, and she didn’t notice. When the bus arrived, I climbed aboard, and I found I could recall every detail. That is rare, because most ordinary days blur together. Why?

There is a familiar story that explains moments like this. It says we used to live in an unhurried world, where attention was natural and abundant; now algorithms break us into distracted pieces. That story has truth, but it oversimplifies. Attention has never been easy. Medieval monks complained about wandering minds during prayer; printers, radio, television, and the internet each triggered moral panics. Human attention has always been fragile. What changes is the texture of distraction, not the difficulty.

The bus stop was different not because I was free from machinery, but because I was in a particular mode. I wasn’t doing a task, seeking information, or capturing an image. I was dwelling beside something, open. Psychologists call this soft fascination: a gentle, involuntary attention that asks nothing of us. It’s why we can watch water or clouds or campfires for hours. It is restorative. A screen demands rapid responses and sharp decisions; a tree simply invites you to stay. We feel fed by a few unhurried minutes of it.

The trouble is that modern life is arranged to starve soft fascination. The average day begins with a phone, moves through a cascade of notifications, and ends with a screen that auto-plays one more episode. Waiting rooms, bus rides, breakfasts, lines—all are filled with inputs. We treat silence and idleness as enemies. A decade ago, a person standing on a street corner might glance at the sky, overhear a conversation, or notice a scuffed piece of architecture. Now they are likely staring at a glowing rectangle. Nothing in the city has changed; only attention has. The result is that we become less acquainted with our own surroundings and, increasingly, less acquainted with ourselves.

Why does this matter? Because attention decides the contents of our lives. Two people can stand on the same street, one rehashing an argument inside his head, the other seeing the light in the trees. Their clocks tick equally, but their inner experiences are wholly different. William James wrote that “my experience is what I agree to attend to.” That sounds passive, but it isn’t. Over time, the things we attend to sculpt the people we become. If we attend mostly to anxieties, we become anxious. If we attend to the absurd, the beautiful, the humble, we realize a life with texture and wonder.

Attention is also an ethical capacity. The great healers of the world are first great witnesses. A nurse reads the subtle tension in a patient’s body; a friend hears the wrongness behind a busy voice; a citizen notices the quiet suffering of people who are hidden in plain sight. To pay attention is the only way to respond to another person and their needs. Simone Weil called attention “the rarest and purest form of generosity.” To give your attention is to give your time and your self. In a world of half-listening and quick replies, that is a form of love.

But paying attention to others begins with paying attention to the present moment, including the roaring interior monologue we all carry. Mindfulness is the exertion of watching thoughts arise without obeying them. It isn’t exotic. It is the habit of bringing your mind back, gently, to the task or scene at hand. Most people avoid this because it is difficult. Brains are restless. They want novelty, reward, drama. A leaf falling will never scream for your attention the way a notification does. Yet a mind that cannot sit with a leaf is a mind that cannot truly sit with anything. The search for tranquility is first the search for patience.

After the bus stop, I tested this. For a week, I took a thirty-minute walk each day with no phone and no audio. I expected to be bored, and I was. The first few days felt uncomfortable. My hand wanted something to hold. My thoughts ran to tasks. Then on the fourth day, I noticed a colony of ants crossing the pavement. I squatted and watched for ten minutes. Ten minutes. A tiny world of little routes and cargoes appeared. The facts are irrelevant; the pause was memorable. Since that day, I no longer walk only to get somewhere. I walk to see what will appear.

This is not to reject technology. I write this essay on a computer; a phone carries me through city maps and rare calls home. The enemy is not the device, but the default relationship to it. The phone is our servant, lover, and jailer. We reach for it when anxious, bored, lonely, or tired. It promises comfort, stimulation, and company. The comfort is usually noise; the stimulation is usually fear disguised as excitement; the company is often hollow. The first step is not dismantling the machine but changing its role. We can disable nonessential alerts, keep the phone out of the bedroom, schedule stretches of deliberate emptiness, notice where we reach for it and set it aside.

Author Jenny Odell has written about paying attention to weeds, pigeons, and parking lots—things we are trained to dismiss. She describes birdwatching as a kind of resistance. Her point is political: large tech companies profit from monopolizing our gaze. To look at the overlooked is to refuse the urgency that sells clicks. It is to recover a strangeness in the world that advertising flattens. The plant that pushes through asphalt, the stains on a curb, the shape of a shadow at noon—these are the costs of the world. They don’t need to be monetized or shared. They just need to be seen.

I also learned to reconsider boredom. For years I fled any idle minute, pulling out a feed as soon as a queue formed. But boredom is not the absence of value; it is the signal that the conscious mind has exhausted its usual material, and a deeper well is available. Daydreaming is not a waste. Writers, composers, and scientists report their best ideas arriving while washing dishes or brushing teeth. The default mode network of the brain is active when we are at rest, making links among memories. By filling every gap with external input, we choke off this process. Constant stimulation is not the same as richness; sometimes it is just noise.

Creativity, after all, needs fallow land. A field grows grain by being left fallow. A mind likewise needs unproductive intervals in which to fertilize itself. I wonder how many ideas we lose because we never allow a long car ride without a podcast, a meal without a video, a walk without a step-counting app. The phrase “I’m bored” has become a curse. Better to bless it: boredom is your imagination knocking on the door.

There is a temporal dimension to all this. Modern culture treats time as a commodity: wasting it is a sin, saving it is a virtue. Yet time is not money; it is the substance of experience. When I rush through a day, I compress it into a nondescript blur. When I linger, I stretch it. Attention is the rate at which we convert time into experience. A minute spent watching a snail move across the pavement can be longer, more vivid, than an hour of automated scrolling. Children understand this. Ask any child about a puddle; they will squat, poke it, throw a leaf, chase a ripple. They are not wasting time; they are collecting minutes. Growing up means picking up the pace, but it also means forgetting the art of lingering. We can relearn it, a puddle at a time.

How, concretely, do we rebuild an impractical talent like attention? There are a handful of measures I have found useful. Carry a physical book or notebook. Leave one earbud at home. Take a different route to work. Try a no-phone morning once a week. Practice naming three details of a room when you enter it. When you meet a friend, rest your phone facedown on the table and resist responding to its vibration. Turn off badges and sounds. Use a paper calendar for important dates. Rent a library book. Go to a museum alone. Sit on a bench for ten minutes without touching anything. You will feel foolish at first; the fool is the appropriate student. Maybe you will notice a window box of flowers, a worn brick, a pattern of roof tiles, a cat sleeping on a car. Attention thrives on specificity. It hates generalities.

Attention also returns us to the more-than-human world, which is where ecologists say our wellbeing begins. A walk among trees lowers heart rate; a glimpse of water calms; soil microbes even lift mood. But none of these effects can penetrate if you are staring at a slab. I began to learn the names of local birds and trees. Naming is an act of attention. It feels like unlocking a door. Once you know that the small fast bird is a wren and the big slow one is a crow, the landscape begins to speak. The naturalist Rachel Carson wrote that if you are curious, you will be educated. Curiosity is attention with a sense of wonder. You don’t need to be an expert; you only need to be willing to ask what that is, and then wait for the answer.

Habits of attention are not private. They affect relationships. When a friend tells us something and we automatically glance at our phone, we send a message: you are not enough. When we sit across from someone but still inhabit the bubble of our notifications, we are absent. The lapse is tiny, but repeated, it becomes gravity. The inverse is also true: a person who looks steadily at you, who asks a real question and waits, who doesn’t immediately check a message — that person makes you feel solid and seen. We can practice this. We can leave our phone face down. We can fight the urge to interject. We can let silence sit there. With practice, the other person’s face becomes a landscape, and their voice becomes a reliable map.

I want to suggest, finally, that attention is love’s workmanship. We tend to think of love as a feeling, but love is mostly an orientation. To love a person is to know what matters to them, to remember their small preferences, to notice fatigue before they mention it. None of that is possible without attention. It is the difference between a caregiver who mechanically performs tasks and one who sees the real human. Caring for another person is a series of attentions: a bedpan, a touch, a shared memory. The deepest praise we can offer anyone is to notice them fully.

My notebook has become my tool for reskilling attention. Whenever I see something odd or lovely, I jot a few words: a cat blinking from a porch, a cloud shaped like a whale, the first cool breeze after heat, a stranger’s laugh, a fresh puddle reflecting the sky. The entries are worthless in any market. Yet they are a record of an examined life. When I flip through the notebook later, the day returns with a clarity that a photo album rarely gives. Photographs freeze a single frame; a written note translates the moment back into the senses.

The season has turned since the bus stop. The tree is bare now, a skeleton of branches. I have seen it in every stage: green, yellow, red, stripped. Familiarity might dull attention, but it shouldn’t. Each day’s light is different. Sometimes the branches look like veins; other times they look like cracks in the sky. There is no end to what a single tree can give if you look honestly. The same is true for a street, a room, a person. The world is endlessly multifarious, but our mode of seeing is often poor. We see through templates: “tree,” “sunset,” “homeless person,” “that guy.” Attention dissolves templates. It sees particulars.

What I gained at the bus stop was not information. It was a reminder that reality is not boring; we merely shift our attention away from it. The synapses of the brain and the rhythms of the city are both full of unexpected mutations. The question is whether we will meet them. We like to imagine we are catching up on life by checking our feeds, but those feeds are manufactured simulations of life, edited for maximum effect. Meanwhile, the real thing runs quietly on the other side of the glass. It runs in kitchens, bus stops, offices, hospitals, forests, schools. There is no shortage of meaning; there is only a shortage of regard. We can restore regard by small acts: putting the device in the drawer, going outside without entertainment, spending time with people and giving them your eyes, reflecting on what your neighbor is carrying, lingering over a meal, noticing the spiderweb in the corner, asking a child what she sees in a puddle.

At the end of the day, attention is not a technique or a morality. It is the posture of being alive. To be alive is to be drawn to light, warmth, noise, movement; but it is also to be able to stop and receive. The philosopher Iris Murdoch described love and attention as the effort to undo the veil of selfishness. There is no veil so thick as the one woven by our endless self-referential devices. Tearing a hole in it is simple, though not easy. Look up. Listen. Stay. Stop telling yourself what the world is and let it tell you. The tree is still there. It has always been there. You will see it as soon as you are willing to be bored, curious, and open.
